items.name: First peoples, maize & the Archaic
items.description: People reached Mexico by the end of the Ice Age: the skeleton of a teenage girl (Naia) in the flooded Hoyo Negro cave of Quintana Roo is about 12,000–13,000 years old. In the Archaic, foragers in caves such as Guilá Naquitz (Oaxaca) and the Tehuacán valley grew squash about 10,000 years ago, and maize was domesticated from teosinte in the Balsas River valley about 9,000 years ago. Villages with pottery spread after about 2000 BCE.

items.name: Olmec & Early Civilisations
items.description: The Olmec (c. 1500–400 BCE) were Mesoamerica's 'mother culture' — the first complex civilisation in Mexico, producing colossal stone heads, a calendar system, and the concept of the ballgame. They influenced all subsequent Mesoamerican cultures. The Maya developed independently in southern Mexico and Central America, producing the most sophisticated writing system and astronomical knowledge in the pre-Columbian Americas.

items.name: The Olmec heartland: San Lorenzo, La Venta & Tres Zapotes
items.description: On the Gulf Coast lowlands of southern Veracruz and Tabasco the Olmec built the first great Mesoamerican centres. San Lorenzo peaked about 1200–900 BCE; La Venta, on an island in the Tonalá river swamps, followed about 900–400 BCE with its clay pyramid and buried jade offerings. Seventeen colossal basalt heads are known. Tres Zapotes outlasted both, and its Stela C carries one of the earliest Long Count dates (32 BCE).

items.name: Monte Albán & the Zapotec state
items.description: Around 500 BCE the Zapotec founded Monte Albán on a levelled mountaintop above the Valley of Oaxaca, one of the first cities in the Americas. Its carved "danzantes" and early glyphs record war captives; by the last centuries BCE it ruled the valley and took tribute from outlying valleys such as the Cuicatlán Cañada. Monte Albán peaked in the Classic (about 200–700 CE) with ties to Teotihuacan, then declined and was largely abandoned by about 850. Zapotec power moved to valley towns such as Zaachila and Mitla.

items.name: Teotihuacan, city of the gods
items.description: Teotihuacan, in the north-east of the Basin of Mexico, grew from about 100 BCE into one of the largest cities in the world, with perhaps 100,000 people or more at its height around 450 CE, laid out on the Avenue of the Dead with the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon. Its influence reached the Maya: in 378 Siyaj K’ak’ arrived at Tikal and installed a new king. The city’s centre was burned around 550 and its population dispersed.

items.name: Teotihuacán & Toltec
items.description: Teotihuacán, near modern Mexico City, was the largest city in the pre-Columbian Americas at its height (c. 150–650 CE) with a population of 125,000–200,000 — one of the world's great cities. Its Pyramid of the Sun is one of the largest pyramids ever built. The city's collapse (c. 550–650 CE) remains mysterious. The Toltec city of Tula dominated central Mexico (900–1150 CE) and heavily influenced the Aztecs.

items.name: Classic Maya kingdoms: Calakmul, Palenque, Toniná & Yaxchilán
items.description: The southern Mexican lowlands were home to some of the strongest Classic Maya kingdoms. The Kaanul (Snake) dynasty ruled from Dzibanche until it moved to Calakmul around 635; under Yuknoom Ch’een II it led a network of allies against Tikal until Tikal defeated it in 695. Palenque (B’aakal) reached its peak under K’inich Janaab’ Pakal (615–683), buried in the Temple of the Inscriptions. Toniná captured Palenque’s king in 711, Yaxchilán’s Shield Jaguar and Bird Jaguar raised its carved lintels, and Bonampak’s murals date to about 790. Toniná’s monument of 909 carries the last Long Count date.

items.name: Northern Maya cities: Cobá, Edzná & the Puuc
items.description: In the north of the Yucatán peninsula, Cobá built a network of raised white roads (sacbeob), including one of about 100 km to Yaxuná, and Edzná in Campeche built canals and its five-storey palace. From about 800 the Puuc hills flourished: Uxmal, Kabah, Sayil and Labná, with mosaic façades of Chaak masks. Uxmal’s great buildings date to around 900, under a ruler called Lord Chaak.

items.name: Epiclassic cities: Xochicalco, Cacaxtla & Cholula
items.description: After Teotihuacan fell, fortified hilltop cities filled the gap in central Mexico. Xochicalco in Morelos carved its Temple of the Feathered Serpent; Cacaxtla in Tlaxcala painted Maya-style battle murals; and Cholula kept growing around its Great Pyramid, the largest pyramid in the world by volume. These cities traded and borrowed art across Mesoamerica before the Toltecs rose.

items.name: El Tajín & Classic Veracruz
items.description: El Tajín, in the hills of northern Veracruz, was the great city of Classic Veracruz culture, at its height about 850–1150. It is famous for the Pyramid of the Niches and for at least 20 ballcourts, carved with scenes of the ballgame and sacrifice. It was burned and abandoned in the 13th century. In the Postclassic the Totonac held the central Gulf coast, with their capital at Cempoala.

items.name: Chichén Itzá
items.description: Chichén Itzá became the dominant city of northern Yucatán after the southern Classic collapse, at its height about 900–1050. Its Temple of Kukulcán (El Castillo), Great Ballcourt, Temple of the Warriors and the Sacred Cenote mix Maya and central Mexican styles, long linked with Toltec Tula. It declined in the 11th–12th centuries, though the cenote remained a pilgrimage site.

items.name: Tollan (Tula) & the Toltecs
items.description: Tollan, the Toltec capital at Tula in Hidalgo, grew from about 900 into a city of perhaps 30,000–40,000 people, with its Pyramid B crowned by giant warrior columns (the Atlantes). Later Aztec tradition remembered the Toltecs as master craftsmen and Topiltzin Quetzalcoatl as their priest-king. Tula was burned and abandoned around 1150, and the Mexica and other Nahua lords later claimed Toltec descent.

items.name: Mixtec kingdoms & Tututepec
items.description: The Mixtec of western Oaxaca ruled many small kingdoms (yuhuitayu) whose genealogies and wars are painted in screenfold codices such as the Zouche-Nuttall. The best known ruler, Eight Deer Jaguar Claw (1063–1115), of Tilantongo, founded his power on the Pacific coast at Tututepec. Tututepec grew into the largest Mixtec kingdom and was never conquered by the Aztecs, who took Coixtlahuaca and much of the Mixteca highlands from 1458. Pedro de Alvarado took Tututepec in 1522.

items.name: Mayapán & the Maya provinces of Yucatán
items.description: Mayapán, a walled city south of today’s Mérida with a copy of Chichén Itzá’s Castillo, ruled northern Yucatán from about 1220 under the Cocom lords with a council of noble families. Around 1441 the Xiu and others rose against the Cocom and sacked Mayapán. Yucatán then split into about sixteen rival provinces (kuchkabal), such as Maní of the Xiu, Sotuta of the Cocom, Ekab, Cupul and Chetumal, which the Spanish found in the 16th century.

items.name: Aztec Empire
items.description: The Mexica (Aztecs) founded Tenochtitlán on an island in Lake Texcoco in 1325. Through the Triple Alliance with Texcoco and Tlacopan, they built an empire controlling most of central Mexico. Tenochtitlán was a marvel of urban planning: population 200,000–300,000, larger than any contemporary European city. Hernán Cortés's small force, allied with subject peoples who resented Aztec rule, and devastating European diseases conquered the empire by 1521.

items.name: The Purépecha (Tarascan) state
items.description: Around Lake Pátzcuaro in Michoacán, the Purépecha lord Tariácuri united the lake towns in the 14th century, and his heirs built the Tarascan state, with its capital at Tzintzuntzan from about 1450. It was the Aztecs’ great western rival, with copper and bronze tools and weapons, and around 1479 it destroyed an Aztec army sent by Axayacatl. Its last king, Tangáxuan II, submitted to the Spanish in 1522 and was executed by Nuño de Guzmán in 1530.

items.name: Tlaxcala, Metztitlán & the unconquered
items.description: Not all of central Mexico paid tribute to Tenochtitlan. Tlaxcala, a republic-like confederation of four Nahua altepetl (Tepeticpac, Ocotelulco, Tizatlán and Quiahuiztlán), was ringed by Aztec lands and fought them in the ritual “flower wars”. The Otomí lordship of Metztitlán in the Hidalgo sierra and the Yopi of Yopitzinco on the Guerrero coast also held out. In 1519 Tlaxcala allied with Cortés, and its warriors were key to the fall of Tenochtitlan.

items.name: The Triple Alliance builds an empire
items.description: In 1428 Tenochtitlan under Itzcoatl, Texcoco under Nezahualcoyotl and Tlacopan defeated Azcapotzalco and formed the Triple Alliance. Moctezuma I (1440–69) carried its wars to the Gulf coast and the Mixteca (Coixtlahuaca, 1458); Axayacatl (1469–81) took Tlatelolco but lost to the Tarascans; Ahuitzotl (1486–1502) rededicated the Templo Mayor in 1487 and reached the Isthmus and Soconusco. By Moctezuma II’s reign it took tribute from about 38 provinces, listed in the Codex Mendoza, while Tlaxcala, the Tarascans and Tututepec stayed independent.

items.name: The Spanish conquest of Mexico
items.description: Hernán Cortés landed on the Veracruz coast in 1519, won the Totonac of Cempoala and then Tlaxcala as allies, and entered Tenochtitlan in November. Driven out on the Noche Triste (June 1520), he returned with tens of thousands of indigenous allies while smallpox swept the city, which fell on 13 August 1521. Spanish captains then took Oaxaca, Tututepec and the Gulf coast (1521–22), Chiapas (1524–28), Michoacán and, with Nuño de Guzmán’s brutal campaign, Nueva Galicia in the west (1530–31). The Mixtón War (1540–42) was the last great rising of the west.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire

items.name: Colonial New Spain
items.description: New Spain became Spain's richest colony. Silver mines at Zacatecas and Guanajuato produced enormous wealth. The indigenous population collapsed catastrophically due to disease (from perhaps 25 million to 1 million within a century). A complex caste system developed. The Catholic Church built magnificent baroque cathedrals and ran extensive missions. Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz (1648–1695) was one of the colonial era's great writers.

items.name: The Montejo conquest of Yucatán
items.description: Francisco de Montejo’s first entries into Yucatán (1527–28 and 1531–35) failed against the Maya provinces. His son Francisco de Montejo the Younger founded Campeche (1540–41) and Mérida on the ruins of T’ho in 1542, and Valladolid followed in 1543 and Salamanca de Bacalar in 1544. The Great Maya Revolt of 1546–47 was crushed. Southern Campeche and the Lacandon forest stayed outside Spanish control for another 150 years.

items.name: Silver & the Chichimeca frontier
items.description: Silver strikes at Zacatecas (1546) and Guanajuato (1550s) drew Spanish miners north into the lands of the semi-nomadic peoples the Spanish called Chichimecas. Their raids on the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro began the Chichimeca War (about 1550–1590), ended by a “peace by purchase” of food, cloth and land and by Tlaxcalan settler towns. Francisco de Ibarra founded Durango and Nueva Vizcaya (1563); San Luis Potosí (1592) and Monterrey (1596) followed, and Oñate set out for New Mexico in 1598.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Camino Real de Tierra Adentro

items.name: Missions & the far north
items.description: Jesuit missions spread up the Pacific slope from Sinaloa (1591) into Sonora; Eusebio Kino founded the missions of the Pimería Alta from 1687, and Juan María de Salvatierra founded Loreto in Baja California in 1697. On the Gulf side José de Escandón settled Nuevo Santander (Tamaulipas) from 1748. After the Jesuits were expelled in 1767, Franciscans and Dominicans took over the missions, and Junípero Serra set out from Baja California for Alta California in 1769. In the south, the Lacandon forest of Chiapas was entered in 1695.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Spanish missions in Baja California

items.name: Bourbon reforms & the intendancies
items.description: José de Gálvez’s inspection of New Spain (1765–71) began the Bourbon reforms: the expulsion of the Jesuits (1767), the Provincias Internas command for the northern frontier (1776), a royal tobacco monopoly, a standing army, and in 1786 the division of New Spain into twelve intendancies. Silver output reached record highs, and Alexander von Humboldt described the kingdom in 1803–04 as the richest in Spanish America.

sources.title: Wikipedia — José de Gálvez, 1st Marquess of Sonora

items.name: The War of Independence
items.description: On 16 September 1810 the priest Miguel Hidalgo called his parishioners to revolt at Dolores (the Grito de Dolores). After Hidalgo’s capture and execution (1811), José María Morelos led the insurgency and the Congress of Chilpancingo declared independence (1813); Morelos was executed in 1815 and Vicente Guerrero kept fighting in the south. In 1821 the royalist officer Agustín de Iturbide joined Guerrero under the Plan of Iguala, and the Army of the Three Guarantees entered Mexico City on 27 September 1821.

items.name: Independence & Reform War
items.description: Father Miguel Hidalgo's Grito de Dolores (1810) launched the independence movement. After brutal warfare, Mexico achieved independence in 1821. The young republic was devastated by instability: over 50 presidents in 30 years, the disastrous Mexican-American War (1846–48) that lost half its territory, and French intervention (1862–1867) under Emperor Maximilian. Benito Juárez, Mexico's first indigenous president, led Reform War liberals to victory.

items.name: Texas, the US war & the lost north
items.description: Texas broke away in 1836 and was annexed by the United States in 1845. In the Mexican–American War (1846–48) US armies took California and New Mexico and captured Mexico City after the Battle of Chapultepec, where the Niños Héroes died. By the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848) Mexico gave up about half its territory, and the Gadsden Purchase (1853–54) sold southern Arizona and New Mexico.

items.name: The Caste War of Yucatán
items.description: In 1847 Maya peasants in eastern Yucatán rose against the Yucatec elites who had taken their land, and nearly drove them from the peninsula. In the east, Maya rebels founded Chan Santa Cruz (now Felipe Carrillo Puerto) around a “Talking Cross” and kept an independent territory for half a century, trading with British Honduras, until the Mexican army took the town in 1901.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Felipe Carrillo Puerto, Quintana Roo

items.name: La Reforma & the French intervention
items.description: Liberals led by Benito Juárez passed the Reform laws and the 1857 Constitution, which ended church and corporate privileges, leading to the War of the Reform (1858–61). France then invaded: it lost the Battle of Puebla on 5 May 1862 (Cinco de Mayo) but took Mexico City and installed Maximilian of Habsburg as emperor (1864). Juárez’s republic fought on, and after the French left, Maximilian was shot at Querétaro in 1867.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Second French intervention in Mexico

items.name: Porfiriato & Revolution
items.description: Porfirio Díaz's 35-year dictatorship (1876–1910) modernised Mexico through foreign investment while dispossessing peasants. The Mexican Revolution (1910–1920) was one of the first major revolutions of the 20th century, drawing in figures like Zapata, Villa, Carranza, and Obregón. Over a million died. The 1917 Constitution was remarkably progressive: land reform, workers' rights, and curbs on the Church. The PRI party dominated Mexican politics for 71 years.

items.name: The Mexican Revolution
items.description: Francisco Madero’s Plan of San Luis Potosí called for revolt against Porfirio Díaz in November 1910, and Díaz resigned in 1911. Madero was murdered in Victoriano Huerta’s coup (1913); Venustiano Carranza, Pancho Villa in the north and Emiliano Zapata in Morelos fought Huerta and then each other. The 1917 Constitution, with land reform and national ownership of the subsoil, outlasted them all; up to a million or more people died.

items.name: Modern Mexico
items.description: Post-war Mexico industrialised rapidly under PRI rule ('Mexican Miracle', 1940s–70s). The 1985 Mexico City earthquake exposed government incompetence and galvanised civil society. NAFTA (1994) transformed the economy but also unleashed the Zapatista uprising in Chiapas. The PAN broke PRI's 71-year grip in 2000. Drug cartel violence has been Mexico's defining challenge since the 2000s. AMLO's government (2018–2024) and Claudia Sheinbaum's election (2024) continued the 'Fourth Transformation'.

items.name: Tlatelolco, NAFTA & the Zapatistas
items.description: Days before the 1968 Olympics, troops fired on student protesters at Tlatelolco in Mexico City. The 1982 debt crisis ended the oil boom, the 1985 earthquake devastated the capital, and NAFTA took effect on 1 January 1994, the day the Zapatista Army of National Liberation (EZLN) rose in Chiapas. After 71 years of PRI rule, Vicente Fox of the PAN won the presidency in 2000.

sources.title: Wikipedia — North American Free Trade Agreement
Wikipedia — Zapatista Army of National Liberation
